JSON: Name: milp_upl_stockpile_floorwidth Title: A mixed-integer linear programming model for joint ultimate-pit-limit determination and long-term open-pit production scheduling with minimum pit-floor-width, extraction-continuity and stockpile–shortage operational constraints Short Hypothesis: Integrating minimum pit floor width and extraction-continuity constraints into a single MILP that also models stockpile inventory and shortage variables will increase schedule feasibility (fewer infeasible periods) while producing equal or higher net present value (NPV) than a sequential UPL-then-scheduling workflow on the same block models. Related Work: Existing approaches to open-pit planning fall into three broad categories: (1) exact geometric/graph methods (e.g., Lerchs–Grossmann and max-flow) that compute ultimate pit limits but do not jointly schedule multi-period extraction under detailed operational constraints; (2) mixed-integer programming (MIP) formulations for production scheduling that maximize discounted cash flow but commonly assume a pre-defined UPL or omit geometric constraints such as minimum pit-floor width and extraction continuity; and (3) metaheuristic and hybrid methods (genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, tabu search, particle-swarm, augmented-Lagrangian hybrids and LNS-on-MILP) that tackle large-scale or stochastic problems at the cost of optimality guarantees. Limitations across these lines include (a) separation of UPL and scheduling leading to inconsistent block valuation and suboptimal schedules, (b) simplified or missing pit-floor-width and continuity constraints that impair operational realism, (c) inadequate stockpile modeling or absence of explicit shortage penalties that cause infeasible or brittle plans, (d) formulations that do not report feasibility recovery mechanisms when demand exceeds extraction, and (e) scalability and reproducibility issues for exact methods on realistic block models. Prior stochastic MIP work addresses grade uncertainty but frequently still omits the combined geometric and stockpile-shortage modeling required for practical feasibility under varying plant demand. Abstract: This research develops a single mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) framework that jointly determines the ultimate pit limit (UPL) and computes a multi-period production schedule for open-pit mines while enforcing 1:1 slope precedence, minimum pit-floor width, extraction continuity, per-period extraction capacity, plant feed-block requirements and a minimum feed grade. The model optionally includes stockpile inventory and shortage variables with associated holding and penalty costs to resolve infeasibility when demand exceeds production. The main contribution is the integration of minimum pit-floor width and extraction-continuity constraints into a unified, exact MILP together with explicit stockpile–shortage accounting, enabling direct comparison with sequential UPL-then-schedule workflows and heuristic baselines. Expected outcomes are improved schedule feasibility under realistic operational limits, transparent trade-offs between holding cost and shortage penalties, and quantitative sensitivity to pit-floor width and plant capacity. The framework is designed for implementation in standard MILP solvers and supports ablation and sensitivity studies to evaluate operational parameter impacts on NPV and feasibility. Experiments: Datasets: (A) small: the 5×7 block model from the report (single-layer example) with provided BEV and OW matrices; (B) medium: synthetically generated block sets of size 30×30×6 (rows×cols×bench-depth) with three grade-distribution families (low-variance, high-variance, zonal) and 50 stochastic realizations each; (C) large: two publicly-cited open-pit benchmark instances from mine-planning literature (one medium-size, one large-size) converted to the model format. All datasets include block tonnage, grade, recovery, metal price, mining/processing/refining costs. Baselines: (1) sequential: Lerchs–Grossmann UPL determination followed by MIP production scheduling (no floor-width/continuity enforced), (2) MILP_no_floor_continuity: the same unified MILP but with pit-floor-width and extraction-continuity constraints removed, (3) heuristic_GA_stockpile: genetic-algorithm based scheduler with stockpile handling (status-quo metaheuristic), (4) MILP_with_stockpile_only: unified MILP including stockpile/shortage but without floor-width/continuity constraints. Proposed: MILP_full: unified MILP with floor-width, continuity, stockpile and shortage variables. Evaluation metrics: total discounted NPV, feasibility rate (fraction of periods meeting plant demand without positive shortage), cumulative shortage penalty, cumulative stockpile holding cost, average feed grade per period, number of ore blocks extracted per period, solver runtime, peak memory, MIP optimality gap. Experimental setup: implement in GAMS 27.2 or AMPL and solve with CPLEX 12.10 and Gurobi 9.5 for cross-check; hardware: 8-core Intel Xeon or i7 (3.0 GHz), 64 GB RAM; solver settings: MIP gap 0.5% (primary), time limit 7200 s per instance, integer tolerance 1e-6. Repetitions: for stochastic/heuristic baselines run 30 independent seeds per instance; for MILP runs use fixed seeds for presolve/randomization and repeat 5 times to capture runtime variance. Ablation studies: compare MILP_full vs MILP_full minus (a) pit-floor-width constraint, (b) extraction-continuity constraint, (c) stockpile/shortage variables; sensitivity studies: vary pit-floor-width parameter (1–4 blocks), plant capacity (0–4 ore blocks/period), stockpile cost SC ∈ {0.01,0.1,1}× base, shortage penalty P ∈ {0.1,1,10}× base. Statistical analysis: report means, standard deviations, and use paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (α=0.05) between MILP_full and each baseline on NPV and feasibility rate. Outcome measures: confirm or refute hypothesis by testing whether MILP_full yields statistically higher feasibility rate and non-worse NPV than sequential baseline. Risk Factors and Limitations: Scalability: the unified MILP grows rapidly with blocks×pits×periods; binary-variable explosion may make large instances intractable within practical time limits. Solver dependency: results and runtimes depend on commercial solver performance (CPLEX/Gurobi) and presolve; reproducibility may be affected by solver versions. Model infeasibility modes: unrealistic plant demand or tight pit-floor-width parameters can render the MILP infeasible without softening or external adjustments. Sensitivity to penalty coefficients: shortage and stockpile penalty magnitudes can dominate objective values and lead to qualitatively different schedules; selecting realistic penalty values is nontrivial. Data quality/generalization: results depend on accuracy of block grades, costs and recovery; geological uncertainty and stochastic grade variability are not explicitly modeled here, limiting robustness. Operational realism limits: the formulation abstracts many operational details (truck cycle times, fleet scheduling, pushback phasing, haul-road layout, geotechnical bench angles != 1:1, multi-product concentrates) so solutions may require further adaptation for operational deployment. Numerical issues: integer symmetry and weak LP relaxations may cause large optimality gaps or long tail runtimes. Constraint fidelity: the linearized representation of continuity and floor-width is an approximation of real equipment maneuverability and may not capture all site-specific safety/geotechnical rules.
